summary:
Murmansk Oblast stands under the national framework of Russia. The UK Home Office country policy and information note of June 2025 sets out that framework: same-sex sexual activity is not criminalised, but same-sex marriage and gender transition are banned, and the Russian constitution offers no specific legal protections for LGBT+ people. Public expression promoting non-heterosexual relationships or gender transition is punishable under the 'gay propaganda' law by fines or detention of up to 15 days, with repeated offences risking criminal prosecution and up to four years' imprisonment. Trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned in 2023.

Enforcement is federal and applies in full to this oblast. Human Rights Watch reported on 30 June 2025 that Russian courts have issued 101 'extremism'-related convictions for participating in the 'International LGBT Movement' or displaying its alleged symbols. A further 81 people have been convicted of administrative offences for displaying those symbols across 98 court cases since January 2024, mostly in social media posts. The 2023 Supreme Court designation of the movement as 'extremist' opened the way to criminal prosecutions carrying up to 12 years in prison, building on the 2013 'gay propaganda' law.
tangentialFactors:
Between 2022 and 2024 at least 139 people in Russia were affected by enforcement of anti-LGBT+ laws, including convictions, detentions and 'extremism' prosecutions, according to the June 2025 UK country policy note. The same note records that trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned in 2023.

Two enforcement tracks run in parallel: criminal 'extremism' charges carrying sentences of up to 12 years, and administrative offences for displaying alleged movement symbols, which account for the larger share of recent case volume and are largely social-media based.
localsOnly:
Residents of Murmansk Oblast have no route to legal gender recognition. Gender transition is banned nationally, and the constitution provides no specific protections on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity, so residents have no domestic legal remedy of the kind available to them under refugee-convention standards applied abroad.

Russian residents face the same penalties as visitors: fines or detention of up to 15 days for a first propaganda-law offence, criminal prosecution and up to four years for a repeat, and up to 12 years for criminal 'extremism' charges under the 2023 designation.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Murmansk Oblast-level enforcement data is present in the source inventory. Whether this oblast has recorded its own 'extremism' convictions, administrative symbol-display cases or police raids is unresolved, and the figures cited are national totals.

The applicable penalties are sourced to the June 2025 UK country policy note and the 30 June 2025 Human Rights Watch report; oblast-level policing practice, border-post screening of travel documents, and local detention conditions are not sourced here and remain open.
